pending_articles.title: Linking Covariates to State Durations in Dynamic Brain Networks via Hidden Semi-Markov Models
pending_articles.content: Hidden semi-Markov models (HSMMs) provide a flexible framework for studying dynamic functional connectivity because they represent brain activity as transitions between latent network states with explicit dwell time distributions. Although dwell times are often associated with behavioral and demographic variables, these associations are typically assessed only after model fitting using indirect group comparisons, limiting formal covariate modeling and the simultaneous inclusion of multiple predictors. In this work, we extend the HSMM framework by introducing covariate-dependent dwell time distributions through a regression-based formulation, allowing expected state duration to vary with subject-level covariates and enabling direct inference on how these factors relate to state persistence. Model parameters are estimated with an expectation-maximization algorithm, and uncertainty in the dwell-time regression coefficients is quantified using a subject-level nonparametric bootstrap. In simulations, the proposed model accurately recovered covariate effects under both shifted-Poisson and Gamma dwell time specifications, with low bias and variability. We applied the method to resting-state fMRI data from 1,000 UK Biobank participants and found that age and sex were associated with dwell times in a subset of brain states. Together, these results show that modeling dwell-time behavior directly provides a more flexible framework for studying individual differences in brain dynamics, revealing not only which states occur, but also how long individuals remain in them.
pending_articles.author: Shappell, H., Lindquist, M.

pending_articles.title: Electrophysiological Dynamics of Default Network Suppression
pending_articles.content: Distributed brain networks compete with one another in the service of information processing. One dramatic example is antagonism between networks that support internally directed cognition, often collectively referred to as the default network, and networks that orient to external events and drive action. Here we combined within-individual precision functional neuroimaging and intracranial electrophysiology to investigate network competition at high spatiotemporal resolution. In six patients, robust antagonism between networks was established during a target detection task. Network-assigned electrophysiological recordings displayed concordant responses, including in single-neuron firing rates, and further revealed the temporal dynamics of network competition. Networks involved in salience detection and action planning showed early, transient responses that peaked near the participant response. Default network suppression occurred later, reflected in decreases in high-frequency broadband activity and in single-neuron firing rates in response to targets. Examining subcortical regions revealed rapid activity increases in the thalamus and posterior hippocampus aligned to the participant response. Critically, a late evolving, sustained suppression was observed throughout the hippocampus. These findings suggest that, across cortical and subcortical regions, network competition is temporally layered. Furthermore, the hippocampus can be dissociated along its long axis during competition. Such push-pull antagonism may be fundamental to advanced human cognition, and its disruption may underlie mental illness.

pending_articles.title: Sensory experience-induced plasticity of somatostatin interneurons occurs through two-pore potassium (K2P) channels
pending_articles.content: GABAergic interneurons (INs) are powerful modulators of plasticity and learning in cortical networks, but plasticity of INs themselves is not well understood. We studied experience-dependent plasticity in somatostatin (SST) INs, which critically regulate dendritic integration, sensory tuning, and plasticity in pyramidal neurons in sensory cortex. Whether SST INs exhibit experience-dependent plasticity, and by what mechanisms, is unknown. We found that 3 days of whisker deprivation strongly downregulated intrinsic excitability of SST INs in L2/3 of somatosensory cortex, by reducing input resistance. Deprivation also increased mEPSCs onto SST INs. The reduction in intrinsic excitability was caused by an increase in leak potassium current through two-pore K+ (K2P) channels, without changes in HCN, KV1, or KV7 currents, which contribute to plasticity in other IN types and brain areas. Immunohistochemistry showed an increase in TRESK, but not other K2P channels, indicating a novel role for K2P channels in experience-dependent plasticity of interneuron excitability.
pending_articles.author: Bohannon, B. M., Alonso, N. L., Walker, M. G., Wang, M., Kaimaktchiev, K., Yang, C., Feldman, D.

pending_articles.title: BVLab-analyzer: a unified visual toolbox for terabyte-scale whole-brain cell detection, neuron reconstruction, and vascular network extraction
pending_articles.content: BVLab-Analyzer is a standalone graphical software tool for end-to-end analysis of terabyte-scale whole-brain microscopy images. Operating through a zero-code interface, it handles data import (TIFF, BioImageVision, OME-Zarr), deep learning-based semantic segmentation, 3D skeleton reconstruction, and morphological statistical analysis within a unified pipeline. The software supports three target structures—cells, neurons and vasculature—and exports their morphological reconstructions in standard SWC format. To accelerate training data preparation, Smart Annotation tools provide sub-volume interference isolation, coarse-vessel ray tracing, and skeleton auto-interpolation. For inference, optimized block-wise strategies enable a standard 3D U-Net to predict whole-brain volumes up to 12 TB on a single consumer-grade GPU, while an interrupt-and-resume engine ensures fault tolerance during extended computations. By integrating these features, BVLab-Analyzer lowers the hardware barrier for whole-brain analysis and unifies previously fragmented toolchains—from annotation and segmentation to reconstruction and quantification—into a single, accessible software environment.
pending_articles.author: Tingwei Quan

pending_articles.title: Natural language processing for suicidal behavior detection in short Spanish clinical notes from first-contact interviews
pending_articles.content: IntroductionSuicide is a multifactorial phenomenon influenced by social, cultural, biological, and psychological factors, whose early detection remains challenging. According to the World Health Organization, suicide is the third leading cause of death among individuals aged 15–29 years, representing a major public health concern for young populations worldwide. In first-contact clinical settings, screening opportunities are often constrained by limited time, sparse patient information, and operational workflows. This study evaluates the feasibility of detecting suicidal behavior from short Spanish-language texts collected during initial screening interviews.MethodsThe dataset comprises 374 anonymized records labeled as “no suicidal behavior,” “ideation,” “planning,” or “attempt,” with a strong imbalance toward “attempt,” reflecting operational clinical usage rather than population-representative sampling. To address data scarcity, we applied data augmentation methods (Easy Data Augmentation for Spanish, backtranslation, and large language model-based synthesis), validated through statistical analysis and clinician-based plausibility assessments.ResultsExploratory analyses revealed highly constrained and overlapping lexical patterns across classes, indicating the challenging nature of the task. A Support Vector Machine achieved 0.53 macro F1 in binary classification (“suicidal behavior” vs. “no behavior”), while BETO, a Spanish BERT model, reached 0.36 macro F1 in multiclass classification. Under the same text-only conditions, human specialists achieved macro F1 scores of 0.29 and 0.15 respectively; however, these results were based on only 20 real texts evaluated with double annotation across five specialists and should therefore be interpreted cautiously.DiscussionAlthough performance is modest compared to studies using full clinical records, these findings suggest that short-text machine learning could support nonspecialists in first-contact settings. Future work should expand datasets and explore multimodal approaches, including voice and text, to improve clinical applicability and early detection.
pending_articles.author: Ansel Y. Rodríguez-González

pending_articles.title: Transformers for fMRI analysis: from spatiotemporal modeling to brain foundation models
pending_articles.content: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) serves as a pivotal tool for investigating the functional organization and dynamic connectivity of the human brain, indirectly reflecting neural activity through blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signals. However, the high-dimensional spatiotemporal structure, prominent noise interference, and inter-individual variability of fMRI data pose significant challenges for traditional modeling methods in characterizing complex brain functional patterns. In recent years, the Transformer architecture has gained significant traction in fMRI data analysis, leveraging its self-attention mechanism to model global dependencies. It has demonstrated superior performance in tasks such as brain disease classification, functional connectivity modeling, and brain representation learning. Compared to convolutional and recurrent neural networks, Transformers can more effectively capture long-range spatiotemporal dependencies and offer stronger structural scalability and cross-task transfer potential. To systematically map the development of this field, this paper proposes a unified taxonomy for Transformer-fMRI methods based on modeling dimensions. It categorizes existing research into four primary paradigms: temporal modeling, spatial modeling, spatiotemporal joint modeling, and self-supervised learning, providing a comparative analysis of their structural characteristics and applicable scenarios. Furthermore, this paper summarizes the key challenges regarding computational complexity, data dependency, and interpretability, while exploring the integration of neuroscientific priors with large-scale pre-trained models. Finally, we discuss future directions for Transformers in the construction of brain foundation models and their clinical utility.
pending_articles.author: Bocheng Wang

pending_articles.title: Multi-receptor whole-brain modeling reveals affinity-driven chemoarchitectural mechanism of virtual atomoxetine action
pending_articles.content: Linking molecular mechanisms with large-scale brain dynamics remains a fundamental challenge in computational psychiatry. Receptor-informed whole-brain models have provided mechanistic insights into pharmacological interventions, yet they have largely relied on single-receptor topographies that cannot explain the collective response of multiple receptor systems. Here, we combined pharmacological resting-state fMRI with a whole-brain model incorporating cortical expression of adrenergic and dopaminergic receptors to investigate the effects of atomoxetine, a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor that globally elevates catecholaminergic signaling. Using receptor similarity, we first identified a catecholaminergic chemoarchitecture comprising frontal, posterior and temporal networks, providing the neurochemical scaffold for interpreting atomoxetine-induced brain dynamics. Empirically, atomoxetine selectively stabilized functional connectivity dynamics within the posterior catecholaminergic network. Whole-brain modeling revealed that although individual receptor parameters did not differ between conditions, their collective organization converged toward empirical receptor binding affinities. Remarkably, the simulated atomoxetine state was reconstructed from the placebo configuration through a negative reweighting along this receptor-affinity axis. In silico forward modeling showed that this affinity-driven redistribution gave rise to a cortical modulation pattern aligned with a frontal chemoarchitectural gradient, which was sufficient to simulate the observed dynamical and connectivity changes. Together, these findings suggest receptor binding affinity as a key organizing principle linking molecular receptor organization to brain dynamics, providing a model-based, biologically interpretable computational mechanism through which global catecholaminergic perturbations reshape whole-brain function.

pending_articles.title: Music with monaural beats for anxiety reduction and mood enhancement in individuals with moderate trait-anxiety
pending_articles.content: Monaural beats embedded in music are a popular anxiety-relief intervention, yet implementation parameters and efficacy remain poorly understood. Across two studies of online participants with moderate trait anxiety, we tested whether theta-frequency (4–7 Hz) monaural beats in music produce anxiolytic and mood-enhancing effects beyond the same music alone, whether the salience of the beats relative to the music influences effects, and whether the effect of beats generalizes across heterogeneous musical stimuli. State anxiety, valence and arousal were measured before and after a 25-min listening period. In Study 1, participants (N = 207) were randomly assigned to hear music without beats (Music-Only control) or the same piece with monaural beats blended at three different salience levels: Low-, Moderate-, or High-Beatmix. The Low- and Moderate-Beatmix conditions yielded greater anxiety reductions than Music-Only (padjusted = 0.047, β = −0.46, and padjusted = 0.047, β = −0.46 respectively), whereas Music-Only reduced anxiety more than the High-Beatmix condition (padjusted = 0.047, β = 0.42), indicating that overly salient beats might disrupt anxiolytic effects. Time × Condition interactions were not significant for valence or arousal. In Study 2, participants (N = 259) were randomized to one of four stylistically varied tracks, with or without beats at the Moderate-Beatmix level. Averaged across tracks, Beatmix conditions produced greater anxiety reductions (p < 0.0001, β = −0.49) and positive-valence increases (p = 0.029, β = 0.28) than Music-Only. As in Study 1, the Time × Condition interaction was nonsignificant for arousal. These studies provide some of the first evidence that adding monaural beats to music has anxiolytic effects beyond music alone, that efficacy depends on relative beat salience, and that findings replicate across a range of musical tracks.
pending_articles.author: Gianluca Micchi

pending_articles.title: The association between dietary protein intake and mental disorders in older adults: a scoping review
pending_articles.content: BackgroundMental disorders are increasingly prevalent among older adults, significantly affecting their quality of life and overall wellbeing. Recent evidence suggests that dietary factors, particularly protein intake, may play a role in mental health outcomes. However, the association between dietary protein intake and mental disorders in older adults remains underexplored. This scoping review aims to examine the relationship between dietary protein intake and mental disorders among older adults.MethodsThis scoping review was conducted using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). A comprehensive search was performed in three databases (PubMed, Scopus, and ProQuest Health) using predefined keywords and Boolean operators. The inclusion criteria and exclusion criteria were established. Thematic analysis was performed to synthesize and map the evidence across the included studies.ResultsFrom an initial 2,144 records, 13 articles (n = 13) involving older adults were included. Three themes emerged from the thematic analysis: (1) Animal Protein; (2) Plant-Derived Protein; and (3) Mixed Proteins. Both animal and plant protein sources were examined, with generally favourable associations reported for cognitive health. However, findings were inconsistent, particularly for total protein intake, and varied according to protein source and mental or cognitive outcome.DiscussionAssociations between dietary protein intake and mental disorders in older populations are heavily dependent on specific protein sources and the synergistic whole-food matrix rather than the isolated protein quantity. While diverse high-quality protein consumption correlates with preserved mental health, the associations may concurrently reflect residual confounding from healthy-user biases and socioeconomic advantages. The cross-sectional design and lack of quality assessment limit causal inference. Thus, robust longitudinal research and targeted intervention studies are warranted to elucidate the independent neurobiological mechanisms of distinct dietary proteins from overarching dietary patterns.

recently_processed.title: Advancing Embodied Intelligence in Robotic-Assisted Endovascular Procedures: A Systematic Review of AI Solutions
recently_processed.content: Endovascular procedures have revolutionized vascular disease treatment, yet their manual execution is challenged by the demands for high precision, operator fatigue, and radiation exposure. Robotic systems have emerged as transformative solutions to mitigate these inherent limitations. A crucial moment has arrived, where a confluence of pressing clinical needs and breakthroughs in AI creates an opportunity for a paradigm shift toward Embodied Intelligence (EI), enabling robots to navigate complex vascular networks and adapt to dynamic physiological conditions. Data-driven approaches, leveraging advanced computer vision, medical image analysis, and machine learning, drive this evolution by enabling real-time vessel segmentation, device tracking, and anatomical landmark detection. Reinforcement learning and imitation learning further improve navigation strategies and replicate expert techniques. This review systematically analyzes the integration of EI into endovascular robotics, identifying challenges such as the heterogeneity in validation standards and the gap between human mimicry and machine-native capabilities. Based on this analysis, a conceptual roadmap is proposed that reframes the ultimate objective away from systems that supplant clinical decision-making. This vision of augmented intelligence, where the clinician's role evolves into that of a high-level supervisor, provides a principled foundation for the future of the field.

recently_processed.title: A caudate-centered network for alexithymia derived from patients with brain tumors
recently_processed.content: Alexithymia is a trait characterized by impaired emotional awareness. Previous accounts examining the neurobiological underpinnings of this trait have centered on a variety of structures, and alexithymia-causing lesions occur in disparate locations. We use lesion network mapping to derive a neural circuit for alexithymia. In a neurosurgical cohort of 45 patients with gliomas (19 female; aged 18-75 years), we compute each lesion's connectivity to the rest of the brain using a normative connectome (n = 1,000) and relate these connectivity maps to preoperative Toronto Alexithymia Scale scores using permutation testing. Lesions associated with higher alexithymia are connected to a common network that includes the bilateral caudate heads (right greater than left) and the anterior cingulate cortex, peaking in the right caudate head (family-wise error-corrected p < 0.05). The network converges with coordinates from an independent meta-analysis of gray matter volume in alexithymia (13 of 14 coordinates positive; p = 0.0004). Of the three subscales, difficulty identifying feelings localized to this network. Within the striatum, the network spans the executive and limbic subdivisions. These findings suggest a caudate-centered circuit, at the interface of affective and executive systems, that unifies disparate lesion locations.

recently_processed.title: The Relational Capacity Framework: A Lens for AI-Mediated Relationality
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2611.08877v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A growing literature examines the impact of engaging with AI chatbots on our relationality: our ability to form relationships with others, maintain them through life's changes, and exit when needed. Currently, substantial work focuses on purpose-built AI companions (e.g. Replika, Character.AI), with less work investigating socioemotional uses of the more widely-used general-purpose chatbots. In this paper, we present a 100-person investigation into how people engage general-purpose AI for socioemotional needs. Participants' AI uses varied, from practicing specific social skills to seeking additional bandwidth and information as they navigated their social contexts. To explain this heterogeneity, we provide 8 states that describe how AI expands or contracts relationality for people with different levels of skills, bandwidth, and information. We then present a unified conceptual model for the role of technology in mediating human relationality, the Relational Capacity Framework, and outline future research designing appropriate roles for AI in human connection.
recently_processed.author: Emily Tseng, Patrick Gage Kelley, Renee Shelby, Ashley M. Walker

recently_processed.title: Bidirectional Modeling of mmWave Human Signals for Enhancement & Synthesis
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2611.08870v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) is attractive for human-centered robotics in smoke, darkness, and privacy-sensitive indoor spaces: it measures reflections rather than visually identifiable imagery and remains usable without light. Deployed systems, however, face two complementary needs that run in opposite directions. Enhancement starts from a raw range-angle-Doppler (RAD) heatmap, where human returns coexist with nonhuman structure, and aims to isolate the human signal by removing nonhuman returns, yielding a clean RAD input for downstream perception. Synthesis starts from denser human geometry and aims to synthesize natural RAD observations, including environmental and hardware features, thereby expanding scarce supervision data. Although the two tasks reverse direction, both require modeling how human and nonhuman reflections coexist in the same measurement. Among RAD axes, Doppler provides motion information native to the modality, with the potential to support this modeling. We therefore cast both tasks on the dual-domain RAD heatmap and propose HeatWave, which injects Doppler when it is locally reliable, and routes Doppler asymmetrically for enhancement and synthesis within one shared backbone. This design improves both tasks: enhanced observations reduce mean per-joint position error by 11.4% relative to the raw recording, and synthesized samples that replace half of the real radar labels recover most of the activity accuracy lost to the reduced budget. Relative to an unspecialized dual-task heatmap baseline, the enhancement improves motion-critical samples under metallic clutter by 2.3times more than when geometry already suffices, and synthesis follows the same ordering with a narrower spread, providing the community with a research direction more closely aligned with the signal's characteristics.
recently_processed.author: Shuntian Zheng, Hoang Hai Pham, Jiaqi Li, Xiaoman Lu, Shuai He, Yu Guan

recently_processed.title: "I had nobody to turn to": Why LGBTQ+ People Choose (Not) to Use AI Chatbots for Personal Health and Relationship Advice
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2611.08854v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While there is an abundance of research into large language model (LLM) biases against LGBTQ+ communities, far less research has examined how and why LGBTQ+ people choose to make use of AI chatbots. In this work, we examine how LGBTQ+ people choose (not) to use AI chatbots across three domains in which LGBTQ+ users have unique needs: relationship support, mental health support, and gender or sexual health support. We surveyed 73 people (60 LGBTQ+; 13 non-LGBTQ+) on how they interact with AI chatbots and find that participants' access to external resources, privacy concerns, and perceptions of chatbot capabilities shape whether and how they choose to make use of AI chatbots. For instance, some LGBTQ+ participants felt that chatbots might actually be less biased against LGBTQ+ people than the people they know offline. We also find that LGBTQ+ participants report using AI chatbots less frequently than non-LGBTQ+ participants across 15 specific personal health and relationship advice scenarios, citing concerns about AI sycophancy and adverse cognitive side-effects. Recognizing AI chatbots as vital (albeit imperfect) resources for LGBTQ+ people, we recommend researchers consider systemic issues that drive users to AI chatbots and design technologies (AI or otherwise) that prioritize privacy, anonymity, and real human connection.
recently_processed.author: Jacob Hobbs, Ashray Gupta, Dennis Ulmer, Geetanjali Aich, Nolan Golden, Yanan Long, Ian Rios-Sialer, Jennifer Mickel, Morgan Klaus Scheuerman, Rohit Avinash Mujumdar, Virginia K. Felkner, Jordan Taylor, William Agnew

recently_processed.title: Lea: An Agent Backbone for Mathematician-Controlled Formalization in Lean
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2611.08849v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic systems now formalize research-level mathematics in Lean, but they are built for autonomy: the mathematician states a target and inspects a result. The alternative, a general-purpose coding harness, is domain-neutral and must be assembled into a formalization workspace before any mathematics begins. Mathematicians, however, report wanting to keep high-level control over how an argument is decomposed and established. We present $\textbf{Lea}$, a Lean-specific agent backbone for mathematician-facing software rather than a single interface. Lea exposes runs, sessions, and typed events through one application-neutral API, and ships with Lean tooling (blueprints, LSP, Loogle, SafeVerify) already wired. We report two applications built on it: $\textbf{LeaChat}$, a web client for interactive proof authoring, and $\textbf{LeaOverleaf}$, which formalizes theorems annotated directly in an Overleaf document; a session begun in either continues in the other. In a case study, a mathematician outlined a proof of the Durfee square generating function in a few natural-language messages, and Lea produced a complete Lean development from Mathlib alone, following the intended decomposition closely and requiring substantive correction at a single point. Lea and both applications are released as open source so that further mathematician-facing tools can be built on the same backbone.
recently_processed.author: Shaswat Patel, Daniel Aarao Reis Arturi, Kevin Gomez, Jaume de Dios Pont, Jorge Poco, Eduardo V. Teixeira, Sam Westrick, Claudio Silva, Chinmay Hegde

recently_processed.title: Driver Takeovers and Longitudinal Responses Analysis from Naturalistic Driving
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2611.08798v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As Level 2 advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) become more widely used, understanding driver-system interaction is increasingly important for traffic safety. However, limited real-world data make these interactions difficult to study. We present ADAS-TO, a naturalistic dataset of 16,446 takeover clips from 364 drivers across 2,585 different drives. It combines road video, vehicle kinematics, driver inputs, and ADAS status. To analyze takeover behavior, we retained 6,206 manually reviewed takeover events during continued lane keeping or car following. We excluded events in which the driver intentionally changed lanes, turned, or made a stop beyond the ADAS's capabilities (e.g., at a red light or stop sign) shortly after takeover. Drivers began intervening before ADAS disengaged in 65.6% of takeovers involving braking or steering. When the ego vehicle was still closing on a lead vehicle at disengagement, longitudinal safety margins often narrowed further after the transfer to manual control. Among 2,031 such events, 78.5% had a lower minimum time-to-collision (TTC) in the five seconds after disengagement than in the five seconds before it. For events involving braking, the mean TTC trajectory reached its minimum about 1.2 s after disengagement. We model the subsequent braking response using a Gazis-Herman-Rothery (GHR) car-following law. Its median five-second spacing root-mean-square error is 1.34 m with observed lead motion and 1.84 m with predicted lead motion. The fitted model expresses braking as a response to looming, with stronger responses at higher speeds and shorter gaps. Applied before takeover, it shows that greater looming than predicted by the human-response reference is associated with disengagement. These findings support continued assessment of longitudinal safety after ADAS disengagement, while the driver's braking response develops.
recently_processed.author: Yuhang Wang, Hao Zhou
